newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. set to condemn Israeli building in E.Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: U.N. set to condemn Israeli building in E.Jerusalem.

text.p: A General Assembly resolution calling on Israel to rescind plans for a new Jewish neighbourhood in mostly Arab East Jerusalem is expected to be adopted by an overwhelming majority late on Thursday.

The resolution is almost the same as one vetoed by the United States in the Security Council on last Friday after receiving the support of all the other 14 council members. The draft was sponsored by the council's four European Union members -- Britain, France, Portugal and Sweden.

The United States, chief sponsor of Middle East peace talks, joined nearly 50 other speakers in the council debate in criticising Israel's action. But it said the U.N. body was not an appropriate forum for debating issues that should be negotiated directly between Israel and the Palestinians.

Arab states, frustrated by the veto, took the issue to the 185-member General Assembly on Wednesday when almost all 30 speakers in the debate again condemned Israel's plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a tree-covered hill between East Jerusalem and Bethlehem that Israel captured during the 1967 Middle East war. The area is called Har Homa by Israel and Jabal Abu Ghneim by the Palestinians.
Fewer speakers took part in the Assembly debate than in last week's council meetings since a number of participants spoke as representatives of various groups.
The Assembly resolution is sponsored by more than 40 countries including most Arab states, a number of nonaligned countries and all 15 members of the European Union.

It calls on Israel to "refrain from all actions or measures, including settlement activities, which alter the facts on the ground, pre-empting the final status negotiations, and have negative implications for the Middle East peace process."

The resolution also calls on Israel to abide scrupulously by its obligations under the Fourth Geneva Convention on the protection of civilians in time of war, which bars settlements in occupied territory, and urges all parties to press ahead with the peace process.
The only difference from the vetoed Security Council draft is an additional paragraph asking Secretary-General Kofi Annan to bring the provisions of the Assembly resolution to Israel's attention.
The secretary-general normally notifies all delegations of Security Council decisions but not those adopted by the Assembly, where all U.N. members are represented.

The vote comes as the Middle East peace process appears to be in deep trouble, with the Palestinians also objecting to a recent Israeli decision to hand over 9 percent of occupied territory in the first of three scheduled pullbacks, instead of the 30 percent they said they expected.
Tensions have been heightened by an exchange of mutual recriminations between King Hussein of Jordan and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose countries signed a peace agreement in 1994.

Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat has invited U.S., European and Arab envoys to a meeting in Gaza on Saturday to discuss the crisis in a move that Israel regards as another departure from direct negotiations.
